approvedGoal:
This delivery makes the backend more reliable and faster, and gives each a
measure. Reliability comes from deciding the user once, at the transport, and
running a request on NestJS's own mechanisms instead of ours; speed comes from
serving production on Fastify instead of Express.

### Reliability: self-written mechanisms on a request's path

A mechanism we wrote ourselves where the framework already has one is code that
only we keep correct. The measure is how many such mechanisms a request passes
through, counted in the backend source on `origin/staging@5c03c884d`. The target
leaves one place that decides the user and the framework's own mechanisms for
the rest.

| What a request passes through | Today | Target |
|---|---|---|
| places that decide who the user is | 7 — two token checks, `SessionContextService` and the source-connection start route's own, and five contexts built from a bare user id | 1 — `SessionContextService` |
| a WebSocket protocol written by hand on raw `ws` | 1 | 0 — Nest's WebSocket gateway |
| HTTP handlers that write the Express response themselves | 31 | 0 — one exception filter and one response interceptor |
| HTTP routes that change the whole system without an admin check | 3 | 0 |
| ports that serve MCP beyond the machine | 1 — the API port, wherever `HOST` is public | 0 |

### Speed: HTTP throughput and p99 latency of the real backend

The measure is requests per second and p99 latency in milliseconds, per route, on
the real backend. Production runs on Nest's Express adapter today and moves to
Nest's Fastify adapter in this delivery. The target: on the same routes,
Fastify's median throughput is higher and its median p99 no higher, with the
min–max band of each side reported.

The real backend has not been measured yet. Today's only evidence is synthetic: a
small Nest 11 app with a bearer guard and a response interceptor — not Magnis — on
Bun 1.3.13, the version CI pins, two runs per adapter:

| route of the synthetic app | Express req/s, median (min–max) | Express p99 ms | Fastify req/s, median (min–max) | Fastify p99 ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| health | 24,663 (23,337–25,990) | 3 | 29,499 (27,211–31,786) | 2–3 |
| RPC | 10,115 (10,013–10,217) | 8–9 | 10,869 (10,149–11,589) | 7–8 |
| RPC that waits 1 ms | 10,401 (10,323–10,480) | 9–10 | 12,370 (11,126–13,614) | 6–9 |

For plain RPC the two bands overlap, so this benchmark does not show Fastify
faster there; for health and the waiting RPC they do not. Two runs per side are
too few to trust as a band, and the Fastify runs met heavier background load on
the machine (load average 13–19 against 6–9). The plan therefore does not judge
the move on these numbers: D1-S35 measures the real backend on Express before the
move and on Fastify after it, several runs per side, and records the median and
min–max per route.

### How we will know it works

- `git grep -n -E '\bRequestContext\b|requestContextFor|isRequestContext|currentUserFromRecord|CurrentUserValue|interface CurrentUser' -- backend/src backend/test`
  prints nothing; no controller takes `@Res()` or `@Req()`; `express` is
  imported only where the app is composed; axum's rejection strings are gone; the
  source-connection start route and its own token check are gone.
- `/ws` is served by Nest's WebSocket gateway, with no upgrade listener of our
  own. A socket that has not authenticated receives no result and no event, and is
  closed with `4401` after five seconds; a socket's identity is resolved once.
- Production launches on Nest's Fastify adapter. The backend gives the same
  answers on Fastify and on Express — successes and rejections — for health, an
  HTTP RPC, a file upload and download, a conditional asset request, the provider
  callback and a WebSocket RPC, and the compiled desktop backend still boots.
- Measured on the same machine against the Express backend it replaces — at
  least five interleaved runs per side, median and range — the Fastify backend
  serves health, a cheap HTTP RPC and an RPC that reads the database with higher
  throughput and a p99 latency no worse. The numbers are recorded, not asserted by
  a test.
- Sync pause, sync resume and search-ablation prepare refuse a non-admin and
  admit an admin; admin operations stay HTTP-only, with no RPC counterparts.
- An event reaches its owner's sockets and never another user's.
- `/mcp` is not served on the API port; it answers only on its own listener
  bound to `127.0.0.1`.
- In single-user mode HTTP, the WebSocket and MCP act as the default user
  without credentials, and such a backend refuses to boot on a public address or
  on a database that holds any other human user, and refuses a foreign
  `Origin` or a non-loopback `Host` before any effect.
- `bun run check:backend`, the client-core suite and the end-to-end suite pass
  on the finished branch.

approvedGoal:
Build the backend's canonical Agent execution core and make Episodes its
durable working memory. The Agent is the CPU: it accepts work from a user or a
trigger, assembles the smallest sufficient workspace, runs one of three Agent
implementations, commits effects and remains the owner across `idle`, `active`
and `needs_input` until the Episode itself is closed. Graph is long-term memory; an Episode is one durable short-term
reasoning chain and is also a Graph entity; Triggers are work sources;
the AI Models component is a hidden compute peripheral used only by
`MagnisAgent` through its narrow `LLM_RUNTIME` port.

This plan deliberately removes both **Engine** and the ambiguous generic
**runtime** from the Agent abstraction. Magnis, Codex and Claude are three
implementations of the same `AgentAdapter` port. Codex and Claude own native
loops and sessions; Magnis owns the in-process loop and calls
`LLM_RUNTIME` when it needs an LLM. Provider, local/remote routing, credentials,
pricing and the private `CreditService.authorize/charge` path remain behind
AI Models and are not concepts in Agents or Episodes. Reservation and
settlement are removed rather than renamed.

Measured outcomes:

- **One Agent CPU.** `AgentService` owns every long-lived Episode-agent and
  continuously manages the set whose durable state is `active`. User messages
  address one existing Episode; every Trigger firing creates a new child
  Episode. Both enter the same Agent loop only after those distinct ingress
  rules, and neither launches a competing execution for one Episode.
- **One durable working-memory aggregate.** Episode owns transcript, summary,
  active todo, waits, denied actions, entity references, Agent binding,
  external session, pending user-message queue, accepted input cursor and
  immutable execution receipts.
- **One immutable Agent identity.** Episode creation resolves and persists one
  concrete Agent implementation and one complete profile snapshot. Neither can
  be changed for that Episode. The only later binding mutation is an explicit
  model change: it commits immediately without cancelling the current
  execution, while the next claimed execution observes the new revision.
- **One efficient workspace.** `AgentWorkspaceBuilder` packages typed Episode
  working state, active Graph references and the common versioned Tool catalog.
  It does not pre-load Graph or provider-specific memory. The Episode query
  selects one bounded transcript window while required binding, input, todo,
  wait and denial state is always present; there is no adaptive omission
  planner or second omission ledger.
- **One Agent boundary.** `AgentService` selects a private
  `MagnisAgent`, `CodexAgent` or `ClaudeAgent` through `AgentRegistry` and the
  narrow `AgentAdapter` interface. There is no pass-through
  `AgentRuntimeService` or public coordinator with duplicate ownership.
- **One Tool capability.** Magnis callbacks and native Codex/Claude MCP both
  use one execution-bound `AgentExecutionTools` handle returned by the public
  `ToolService`. Catalog, profile, allowlist, durable approval, dispatch and
  cancellation fences are internal parts of that one capability, not separate
  Agent-facing services.
- **One common Search/Graph path.** Every Agent discovers unknown identities
  through Search Tools and hydrates/traverses known identities through Graph
  Tools, all through the same Tool path. Their registered adapters call
  `SearchService` and `GraphService`; workspace and Agent code create no second
  direct retrieval path.
- **Memory follows the Agent implementation.** Magnis alone owns the product's
  `MemoryService` retrieval/extraction capability. Codex and Claude retain
  their own native session memory. Product Memory is not a common Agent tool
  namespace and is not injected into the common workspace.
- **One explicit lifetime owner.** An Episode-agent persists across many user
  messages and adapter executions in exactly one of
  `idle | active | needs_input`. Closing a window only detaches an observer;
  explicit Stop first commits durable stop intent, then joins the live
  execution and returns the same Agent to `idle` without losing transcript,
  todo or queued input.
  Nest boot reclaims durable `active` Episodes; shutdown joins live handles.
- **One honest usage source.** AI Runtime returns normalized terminal
  accounting, Episodes persists it on `agent_turn`, and
  `episodes.usage.query` groups those rows by Episode in SQL. Credit only reads
  and changes the user's stored balance; it never scans Episode history.
  Transcript messages contain no accounting copy, and no Billing report
  service/repository is created.
- **Graph remains a service boundary.** Graph Tool adapters and
  cross-capability application services call `GraphService`, never
  `GraphBatchRepository`, `GraphBatchWriter`, raw Graph SQL or
  `applyInTransaction`. Agent adapters call only `AgentExecutionTools`.
- **The Episode cleanup pays measurable debt.** On
  `origin/staging@4ccabebe3`, `backend/src/services/episodes/` is 4,052 lines.
  The same explicitly counted misplaced files — `episode-summary.repository`,
  `episode-summary.service`, `episode-turn-persistence` and
  `task-todo-reducer` — add 463 lines: **4,515 to at most 3,600 production
  lines**. Moves do not pay the 915-line reduction.
- **Tests prove only what their harness can observe.** Pure rules, Nest
  ownership, PGlite SQL/rollback, real PostgreSQL contention, three adapter
  contracts, client reducers and isolated Playwright stories form one
  traceable ladder.

Non-goals: changing PR #174's landed provider/local adapters, credentials,
pricing, model control plane or Credit internals; creating a Billing/Metering report capability or
deriving usage from `agent_episode_messages`; changing Search ranking/indexing or Graph merge algorithms; redesigning
Memory ranking or Hypotheses; adding a distributed queue or automatically
replaying an indeterminate external side effect after process death; running
multiple simultaneous executions for one Episode; keeping
`engine`, `builtin` or old RPC aliases; changing an Episode's Agent/profile
after creation; or porting retired Rust tests one-for-one.

# mdurl — publish markdown for browser viewing

Tiny tool on u3775 that takes a local `.md` path and returns a Tailscale URL where the rendered document (dark theme + mermaid diagrams) is served.

## Auto-invoke when the user

- asks to "open this markdown in browser" / "show this plan" / "view as a page"
- says "give me a link to <some>.md"
- says "share this doc / report / research"
- uses Russian: "по ссылке", "в браузере", "открой в браузере", "ссылку на этот файл"
- types `$mdurl` or `/mdurl <path>` explicitly

Skip when:

- the user is not on Tailscale (URL won't be reachable)
- the file is not `.md` / `.markdown`
- the file does not exist on this host

## How it works

```bash
mdurl /absolute/path/to/file.md
# -> http://u3775:6420/<user>/<filename-without-ext>
```

Custom slug:

```bash
mdurl /path/to/file.md custom-slug
```

This plan pays three outcomes through one strict ownership boundary:

   Postgres; only the development/test runner may import or start PGlite.

   disposable child processes. The caller chooses how many workers exist and
   which run receives each worker; the plan then reports the actual green
   wall-clock result before and after, without inventing a required speedup.

   researcher can pin a dataset, explicitly create four PGlite workers, map
   four model configurations onto them, run the variants concurrently and
   open the frontend for any selected worker.

approvedGoal:
Build, install and run local Magnis from the public `0xmikko/magnis`
repository without checking out private application source. The public
Tauri/headless shell owns local process orchestration: embedded real
PostgreSQL, ports, paths, health and tray. When the user selects a local
Ollama model, it discovers a local daemon and offers one explicit install or
start action when that daemon is unavailable. The private repository publishes
an opaque, versioned runtime artifact containing the closed backend and
compiled web application.

**Currency: a public checkout can produce the user-facing local program.**

| Payment | Today at `143f6e847` | Done |
|---|---:|---:|
| tracked desktop files owned privately | 101, including 4,358 Rust lines | 0 after a history-preserving move |
| public desktop applications | 0 | 1 Tauri app plus one headless launcher |
| Tauri build hooks that compile private backend/frontend source | 2 | 0; exact artifact input only |
| runtime selections accepted without version + target + SHA-256 | possible | 0 |
| local database engines | embedded real PostgreSQL | remains exactly embedded real PostgreSQL |
| local Ollama setup path | absent | discover existing daemon; explicit user install/start only |
| clean public-checkout build receipts | 0 | one per Stage 0-supported target |

The user gets one installable desktop application. It starts PostgreSQL and
one verified runtime, waits for health and opens the compiled UI. When the
user selects a local Ollama model, the app adopts a ready daemon without
owning it, or offers one explicit install/start action; backend then discovers
and uses the selected model through its existing adapter. `bin/magnis local`
delegates to the same headless launcher, so GUI and developer launch cannot
drift.

This plan deliberately does **not** move PGlite or redesign backend test
ownership. The shell already passes embedded PostgreSQL's URL to the backend,
so it can be moved and distributed against today's external-URL seam while the
independent hermetic-test-runtime plan changes backend internals in parallel.

approvedGoal:
Reviews become **fast, clean, and useful** — three currencies, each
measured at every close-out:

1. **Review time**: rounds to approval. Today: typically 4–6, tail 9,
   converging by exhaustion. Target: **≤ 2 rounds** — round 1 delivers the
   verdict and the enrichment, round 2 confirms (the
   dataset-dump-orchestrator specimen reached ACCEPT-WITH-CHANGES in
   round 2 — the bar is real).
2. **Context pollution**: review-minted noise in plans and agent context.
   Today: many-round plans carry 80–100 `DEC/INV/scn/tst` tokens each —
   the jargon IS the review interface. Target: **review rounds mint zero
   new IDs**; everything addressed to a human is plain sentences.
3. **Effectiveness**: findings that would break the implementation,
   receipt-bearing, per round — against noise findings. Target: every
   blocking finding carries its receipt, and a **NO-CHANGE round is a
   legitimate, honored outcome** (a useful round is one that either finds
   a day-one breaker or honestly finds nothing).

The guardrail underneath (a constraint, not the goal): unauthorized
intent — review-suggested or implementer-invented scope reaching plan or
code without the owner's word — stays at 0, each adopted suggestion
carrying its passport.

The two reviews get their real missions back, and one boundary binds both
(the owner's crystallization, 2026-08-21):

- **Plan review MAXIMIZES the plan.** The reviewer is deliberately
  creative: imagine the code in operation, hunt inconsistencies and
  consequences, and dump them loudly. Two verdict modes only — (a) the
  plan is INCORRECT (inconsistent, breaks security, wrong premise): say
  it brightly and stop; (b) the plan is sound: ENRICH it with the details
  the implementer will need to build the owner's intent with maximum
  quality. Detail of the intent is welcome INSIDE the plan; a NEW intent
  (a service, layer, fallback, durability mechanism, requirement) never
  enters silently — it goes to the owner as a proposal, or it dies.
- **Implementation review asks: are the plan's GOALS achieved?** The plan
  is approved and the tokens are spent — nothing here reworks the plan.
  First question: is the Goal's currency actually paid? Then the output
  splits into TWO LANES (the owner's refinement, 2026-08-21):

  **Lane 1 — done silently.** Everything that makes the work CORRECT in
  its SIMPLEST form without changing the intent — errors,
  inconsistencies, a bicycle where a standard module exists, a needless
  layer — the reviewer fixes itself, rewriting pieces freely. Rewriting
  is not restricted; inventing is. A finding exists for the simplicity of
  correct work, never for its own sake.

  **Lane 2 — said to the human, in human language.** Architectural
  changes and additions are written as a proposal a person will actually
  read: what changes, why, what it costs — two to four plain sentences.
  Never the jargon form ("DEC-18 removes a crash path that could violate
  invariant 8 in test case 2658") — a human skips that, and a skipped
  proposal does not exist.

approvedGoal:
Search exists so an agent receives the smallest sufficient, current and
evidence-backed context for a business task without reconstructing that context
from a flat pile of documents. Modules make Entity fields, collections and
relationships an executable domain language; Graph remains the authoritative
store; Search uses that language together with lexical and semantic evidence to
discover useful entities; the indexer keeps the derived material ready without
making a Graph write wait for a model.

The product hypothesis is deliberately narrower than “graphs beat RAG”:
**for repeated tasks over a large, heterogeneous personal corpus,
module-declared Entity types and relationships applied before the retrieval
limit will improve useful-context retrieval over an equally provisioned flat
hybrid RAG baseline.** This is an explicit inductive bias and query contract,
not a learned neural-network layer. It should win on typed predicates,
cross-source identity and relationship questions; it may tie or lose on small
corpora and open-ended semantic questions.

The currency of this plan is **one canonical product explanation plus 7
useful-context journeys**: six deterministic agent behaviours and one
reproducible product ablation. Before implementation changes Search, Stage 0
publishes the product explanation as a standalone target document: why Magnis
uses typed Entities and modules, what competitors already prove, how agent,
indexing and query flows work, what is implemented today and what remains a
falsifiable hypothesis.

1. **Declared search:** an agent discovers a module-generated tool, uses only
   that module's declared fields, collections, operators and links, and gets
   matching entities without knowing storage columns.
2. **Keyword discovery:** an exact phrase or set of terms finds the best
   matching entities through full-text search, with one long entity unable to
   consume the page through several matching chunks.
3. **Semantic discovery:** a paraphrase finds the right entities through the
   active embedding index and reports the matched chunk, score and channel.
4. **Constrained hybrid discovery:** keyword and semantic ranks combine while
   schema, typed predicates, canonical relationships, caller ownership and
   archive state remain hard constraints before the final limit.
5. **Fresh materialisation:** a new or edited entity becomes searchable through
   the pull-based indexer; a declaration or chunk-policy change rebuilds it;
   an archived, deleted, foreign or opted-out entity cannot influence results
   even while derived rows remain.
6. **Model lifecycle:** an operator changes the active embedding model through
   one observable command; Search never mixes vector spaces, never clears
   Graph facts and never silently falls back while the index is rebuilding.
7. **Typed-search evidence:** a companion deterministic
   flat-hybrid-versus-typed-search retrieval ablation references the existing
   frozen Magnis research corpora without rewriting them and holds corpus,
   local embedding model, chunks, query, result budget and ground truth equal.
   It tests whether the typed arm has zero hard-constraint violations, does not
   regress aggregate `NDCG@10`, and improves the declared-field/relationship
   query group. A failed hypothesis still pays the evidence journey, but blocks
   the product claim instead of being hidden.

Stage 0 pays the canonical product explanation. Every implementation stage
pays complete journeys. Moving a file, renaming a class or deleting Rust-shaped
code pays nothing unless the corresponding journey is GREEN.

Measurable outcomes when the explanation and all seven journeys are paid:

- one canonical `docs/search.md` explains the Magnis Search product,
  competitor baseline, typed-context hypothesis, agent/index/query flows and
  current-versus-target state without requiring the implementation plan;
- one concrete `SearchService` executes global and module-declared discovery;
- every ranked path applies caller, live and eligibility constraints before
  its final rank and limit;
- one index document policy produces the text used by both FTS and vectors;
- every semantic or hybrid hit can identify its winning chunk and excerpt;
- a companion Search-ablation package references the immutable
  prepared-context corpora and carries fixed inputs, deterministic ground
  truth and reported
  `Recall@10`, `MRR`, `NDCG@10`, forbidden-hit rate and returned context size;
- model changes are serial, restart-recoverable and visible through status;
- the **1,146 current lines** of provider, credential, local-model and Billing
  machinery leave Search for the separately owned AI Models capability;
- the **2,598 current lines** of module query language and execution stop
  living under `services/graph/` and become Search-owned without inventing a
  second query grammar;
- no database migration is introduced.

Out of scope:

- GraphService reconstruction, Entity/Link mutations, provenance, actor/audit,
  merge, hypothesis lifecycle, link-contract redesign or traversal
  implementation; those now belong to the separate Graph plan and session;
- physical provider routing, AI SDK adapters, OpenAI/OpenRouter/Ollama
  behaviour, local model installation, credentials, retries, usage, pricing,
  metering and Billing; AI Models owns them behind `EMBEDDING_RUNTIME`;
- authoring a second wire result type or copying SDK contracts inside Search;
  backend-only candidate, page and runtime-port types stay in `backend/src/core`
  and are projected to the existing SDK DTOs at the transport boundary;
- connector ingest, Episode orchestration, prompt budgeting, memory ranking or
  agent engine selection;
- a new vector database, Neo4j, Cypher, a generic query language, a durable
  indexing queue or a Graph-to-Search callback;
- PostgreSQL FTS language/stemming changes, a catalogue-wide rewrite of
  `search.toml`, paid-provider relevance benchmarks or a claim that Magnis
  universally outperforms Microsoft GraphRAG, Graphiti, Neo4j or LlamaIndex;
- external RPC/tool renames and every database migration.

approvedGoal:
Make every external signal provider enter Magnis through one typed, certified
Source capability. Installation, credentials, account identity, child-process
lifetime, sync delivery, actions, health and user-visible status must each have
one named owner and one fail-closed contract.

The primary currency is **seven unsafe ownership paths reduced to zero**:

1. `SourceService` both publishes definitions and manages live pools.
2. replacement activation retires old pools with an unawaited shutdown.
3. a cancelled/timed-out MCP request can remain in `pending` until close.
4. malformed profiles and fetch results silently become valid defaults.
5. auth persists connection/account/sync state separately from its credential.
6. one bad envelope can be skipped while provider progress still advances.
7. catalog packages release through a directory loop, not an artifact-bound
   certification receipt; Telegram has a separate dispatcher and `x-mcp` is
   outside the connector gate.

Measured outcomes:

- **One control plane.** `SourceService` is the application façade.
  `ExtensionService` remains PR #170's sole immutable artifact/install/enabled
  owner. `SourceDefinitionRegistry` owns definitions,
  `SourceRuntimeSupervisor` owns processes, and `SyncService` owns workers.
- **One explicit protocol lane.** Every artifact declares exactly one version
  and authority: `module_sync` or `tools_only`. Production versus development
  fixture and poll versus push are orthogonal declarations. Existing Sync
  Profile v1 remains a supported lane; module-provider v2 is additive. The host
  selects an exact decoder from metadata; it never probes and falls back.
- **One module-owned data contract.** A module declares named provider
  operations and Zod schemas allowed to create its Graph data. Providers
  implement that interface; they do not define Magnis's canonical schema.
- **One account transaction.** The existing opaque `UnitOfWork` coordinates
  the Source, Secrets and Sync repository participants, so encrypted credential,
  connection, accounts and initial sync rows become visible together without
  moving vault ownership into Sources. Failed Add exposes no generation. Failed
  Repair preserves durable account membership, provider progress and Graph history in
  `auth_required`, while the old credential generation remains fenced and no
  credential fallback is attempted.
- **One supervised binding owner.** `module_sync` uses
  `(sourceId,userId,accountId,artifactHash,accountGeneration)` and a worker adds
  `(surface,syncRowId)`. Credentialless `tools_only` uses one deployment key
  `(sourceId,artifactHash,authority=tools_only)` and creates no account/worker.
  Start is idempotent; stop, replacement and shutdown are awaited; all calls
  are bounded and cancellable.
- **One lossless page rule.** A page is strictly decoded, applied as one module
  batch and only then advances provider progress. Recovery is at-least-once and
  idempotent; this plan makes no exactly-once claim.
- **One certification gate.** The 13 current source directories plus shared
  SDK/testkit are discovered from manifests. Every release artifact produces a
  sidecar receipt bound to package/definition hashes, protocol, authority,
  module-interface hashes and scenario versions. Today only Google and X invoke `runSourceContract`; Anysite merely
  mentions it, while Telegram, Local, `x-mcp` and the mocks use bespoke or no
  shared contract coverage.
- **One honest trust statement.** Certification proves compatibility, not
  sandboxing or publisher trust. Shipping sync providers remain curated
  privileged code. Raw third-party MCP enters only `tools_only` unless a
  curated module adapter and matching receipt grant sync authority.
- **A smaller capability.** The five production zones hold 85 TypeScript files
  / 10,623 lines on the pinned baseline. The target is at most 55 files / 9,000
  lines after deleting generic commands/profiles, duplicate auth/connection
  orchestration and duplicate host dispatch. Moves do not pay the reduction.

Non-goals: replacing PR #170's content-addressed artifacts, accepting arbitrary
MCP tool lists as sync sources, changing Graph merge semantics, creating a
distributed queue, promising exactly-once external effects, making live vendor
tests CI-blocking, or removing certified v1 `magnis.sync.*` operations as a
side effect of introducing v2. Undeclared compatibility aliases still fail.

approvedGoal:
One Workspace capability owns the complete path by which a user's data leaves
Magnis and comes back. The same canonical document and the same import method
serve four callers: the authenticated client, `magnis db dump/restore`, new-user
template provisioning, and eval seeding.

The plan's currency is the **legacy transfer surface** measured after PR #194:

- three owners (`DatasetService`, `WorkspaceSnapshotService`,
  `WorkspaceService`) become one Workspace capability; the first two class
  names and both legacy capability directories disappear;
- 38 TypeScript files / 5,685 lines across `services/dataset/`,
  `services/workspace-snapshot/`, and `services/workspace/` become at most 12
  transfer-owning files / 4,800 lines across their honest owners, with no
  second codec, catalog, lifecycle, or transaction coordinator;
- 48 inbound source-file/directory edges into the two legacy directories become
  zero;
- the three `dataset.*` RPC methods stop being the user-facing import/export
  surface: Workspace gets two SDK-described authenticated HTTP operations, and
  the one eval-only action moves to Eval;
- the four known post-#194 integrity gaps are closed before any new caller is
  allowed onto the format: nullable graph values and entity aliases round-trip,
  export refuses dangling references, and repositories no longer type-import
  upward from their transfer service.

The standard-user journey is concrete: an operator signs in as any deliberately
curated user, exports that user's workspace through the same client contract,
publishes the exact bytes, and pins their locator plus SHA-256 as the deployment
template. A newly created user pins that exact template atomically on its user
row and imports it with newly allocated IDs. Production never live-copies rows
from a “template user” and never needs that source user to remain present.

approvedGoal:
Magnis gives one frontend a predictable way to connect to any local or remote
server: ask who the workspace is, use the one authentication method it
declares, load the current user, and only then mount the application. A saved
connection never borrows a session, profile or server identity from another
workspace.

The currency is **one complete trusted workspace journey**:
`connect → identify → authenticate → load profile → work → switch/reload → logout`.
Its final receipt runs that journey against two independent servers and proves:

- **1/1 persistent workspace identity** per database: a stable id and a
  non-empty admin-editable name; the public response also reports the configured
  `singleUser | multiUser` membership mode and one
  `open | google | password` authentication method;
- **one short public response**, `GET /api/workspace`, before login and **one
  short protected response**, `GET /api/users/me`, after login; public
  discovery contains no graph or indexing counts;
- the protected `UserProfile` returns authoritative profile/admin state plus
  both the current user's and the whole workspace's entity, link, indexable and
  indexed counts; a database failure remains an error rather than a fabricated
  zero;
- **34 → 0 admin-only RPC operations**: the original 21 deployment mutators,
  `source.appconfig.list`, and the 12 AI runtime/credit administration methods
  from the merged staging control plane move to audited Nest REST controllers;
  workspace name and user role administration are REST-only from birth;
- **19 → 0 unguarded deployment mutators** and **37/37 admin REST operations**
  reject an anonymous caller with 401 and an ordinary user with 403 before any
  side effect, while an admin reaches the owning service;
- **184 → 150 native RPC operations**: the remaining RPC surface is for
  authenticated application/user work, with no admin policy branch and no
  role trusted from a token or socket snapshot;
- **6 → 0 `UserRepository` imports outside `services/users/`**:
  `UsersModule` exports `UsersService`, while persistence remains private;
- **48/48 operation-context consumers** use `currentUser.id`, and **3/3 raw
  WebSocket command paths**—captured RPC, fallback RPC and `chat.stream`—load
  the current database user for that command;
- every saved session is keyed by `(connectionId, workspaceId)`; changing the
  server behind a URL forces authentication again.

All new or touched TypeScript identifiers and JSON fields are camelCase. This
plan does not rename unrelated existing RPC ids; that repository-wide protocol
cutover remains a separate change.
